title: Tolkāppiyam
description: The oldest surviving and most authoritative Tamil grammar. It establishes the five-fold grammar (ஐந்திலக்கணம்) including Eluttu, Col, Poruḷ, Yappu (Prosody), and Aṇi. It is largely indigenous with minimal external influence.

title: Vīracōḻiyam
description: Written by Buddhist scholar Puttamittiraṉ during the Chola period. First major grammar to systematically incorporate Sanskrit grammatical structures, terminology (kāraka, sandhi, dhātu, etc.), and poetics while describing Tamil. Contains a dedicated Yāppatikāram (Prosody chapter).

title: Yapparuṅkalam & Yapparuṅkalakkārikai
description: Authored by Jain scholar Amitasāgara. Dedicated treatises on Tamil prosody (Yappu). They represent the peak of indigenous Tamil metrical theory with some later Sanskrit influences in structure.

title: Taṇṭiyalaṅkāram
description: Tamil adaptation of Sanskrit Daṇḍin's Kāvyādarśa. Focuses on alaṅkāra (rhetoric and figures of speech). Reflects growing Sanskrit literary influence during the Chola period.

title: Nannūl
description: Authored by Pavaṇandi Munivar. The most widely used Tamil grammar after Tolkāppiyam. Clear five-fold structure with an excellent Yāppatikāram section. Less Sanskritized than Vīracōḻiyam and more accessible.

title: Sanskrit Chandas Influence on Tamil Yappu
description: From around 600 CE, Sanskrit prosody (Chandas) began influencing Tamil Yappu. Key adoptions include syllable counting (akṣara), mora (mātrā), fixed line lengths, and metres like viruttam (from vṛtta). However, the core acai-based system remained uniquely Tamil and indigenous.

title: Tamil Yappu vs Sanskrit Chandas, Latin & Greek Prosody
description: Tamil Yappu uses a unique acai (metreme) system (nēr & nirai). Sanskrit Chandas is based on akṣara + gaṇa. Latin and Greek prosody are quantitative (long/short syllables) and heavily influenced each other. Tamil prosody developed independently with its own rhythmic logic and toṭai (alliteration) emphasis.
